title: Smj Nonwaivability On Appeal
subject: Civil Procedure
subtopic: SMJ is nonwaivable and may be raised for the first time on appeal
stem: On appeal from a final judgment entered against him, Caleb raised a jurisdictional defect for the first time: when Mary filed her state-law boundary-dispute claim in federal district court, both Caleb and Mary were domiciled in the same state, and she had asserted no federal cause of action. Mary argues the defect is waived because Caleb failed to raise it before or during trial. How should the court of appeals treat the objection?

choices.A: Consider it only if Mary concedes that federal jurisdiction was lacking.
choices.B: Consider it, because lack of subject matter jurisdiction may be raised at any time, including for the first time on appeal.
choices.C: Reject it, because all jurisdictional objections are waived when not raised before or during trial.
choices.D: Reject it, because entry of a final judgment in the district court cures any prior defect in subject matter jurisdiction.

rightExplanation: Federal subject matter jurisdiction is a threshold, non-waivable requirement. Rule 12(h)(3) codifies the principle that a court must dismiss whenever it appears that SMJ is lacking, regardless of when the defect is raised. Neither party consent, litigation to judgment, nor failure to object in the trial court can create or preserve jurisdiction the court never had. The court of appeals must consider Caleb's objection. If jurisdiction was indeed absent — co-domicile, no federal claim — the case must be dismissed without prejudice.

wrongExplanations.A: Subject matter jurisdiction cannot be created or waived by party agreement. Mary's concession that jurisdiction was lacking would be consistent with the outcome but is not required before the court addresses the issue. The court must consider SMJ whenever it appears to be absent, sua sponte if necessary.
wrongExplanations.C: The waiver rule under Rule 12(h)(1) applies to personal jurisdiction, improper venue, insufficient process, and insufficient service of process — defenses that protect party interests and may be forfeited. Subject matter jurisdiction protects the court's institutional authority and may never be waived or forfeited by a party's litigation conduct.
wrongExplanations.D: A final judgment does not retroactively create subject matter jurisdiction. A court without SMJ lacked the power to enter a binding judgment from the outset. Finality principles such as claim preclusion presuppose a court with proper authority; they do not cure the absence of it.
